429.t: Tony Jackson, Pretty Baby, and Chicago pianists and the Pekin Theater
429.s: Jackson wrote Pretty Baby in Chicago around 1911-12; Compton names other pianists and the Pekin Theater where his wife starred.
429.ch: Chicago pianists and New Orleans bands
429.q: No, he didn't have them in those days. He didn't start them until later on in Chicago, around 11, 1911 and 12. He was playing at the Elite number two because I was playing at the Elite number one. And Tony wrote Pretty Baby. Nothing like you ever heard it though.

429.t: The Elite clubs on State Street and Tony Jackson's funeral
429.s: Addresses of Elite No. 1 and No. 2, the cafe bands there, and Tony Jackson as the featured star.
429.ch: Chicago pianists and New Orleans bands
429.q: Just a cafe band. A combination of lines. Carnet, you'd see a Carnet tonight maybe with him. Or Trumon tomorrow night you'd go and see a band or something else. Because Tony was featured. He was a star. I played at Tony's funeral.

76.t: Tony Jackson and the piano players of New Orleans' 25 club
76.s: He went to Chicago wanting to hear Tony Jackson, whose fame he knew from the '25' where New Orleans piano players and pimps hung out. Marge never heard Jackson.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: Yes. Oh, I'd heard of him from New Orleans because that's all you could hear. You see the crowd where I hung out, you see I lived way up town. I used to, Steve Lewis used to bring me down to '25.' That was a place where piano players in the afternoon would hang out. And all of them were sharp and…

76.t: Hearing Tony Jackson at the Deluxe Cafe
76.s: Red Batiste took Zutty to hear Tony Jackson upstairs at the Deluxe Cafe in Chicago, playing beautiful non-jazz music such as Pretty Baby.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: He was playing in the Deluxe Café upstairs. And Red (P) (O) (Batiste) because he knew Tony, and he knew I wanted to hear Tony. And Red (P) (O) (Batiste), he worked for the NapolitW brothers. They called it the Little Club in New Orleans. And I told him that I wanted to hear Tony and he take me out…

259.t: Clarinet, bass and piano players with Dimes; early pianists
259.s: He names the clarinetist (Blind Freddy), the bassist T-Boy, and talks about pianists such as Victor Viall, Tony Jackson and Buddy Christian.
259.q: Well, we just had one kind of player. So who was he? Who was the clarinet player? Oh, uh, Blind Freddy. Blind Freddy. Yeah. I see. Blind Freddy was a clarinet player at that time. Bass? T-boy. He called him Eddie Gilmore. He called him T-boy. He worked out by T-boy. Let's see. Now uh... Fetty Boo…

738.t: New Orleans piano players who made the rounds of the houses
738.s: Asked if he spoke to Jelly Roll, Zutty says he only saw him; a handful of piano players made the rounds of the houses.
738.ch: Jelly Roll Morton in Chicago and early sightings
738.q: they had about five or six

620.s: He remembers Tony Jackson as a fine pianist who played in the district; he himself never worked a district house regularly.
620.q: Tony Jackson was a good piano player. Yeah, Tony Jackson was a good piano player. In fact, Tony Jackson was the only piano player I would sing. The first one I would sing when he played.

2.t: Tony Jackson and Morton's left hand
2.s: Tony Jackson as pianist and composer, Al Rose's album, and Jackson's job at a segregated club.

77.t: The Elite Number Two and Tony Jackson
77.s: At the Elite, owned by Tenan Jones who sold her a $40 ring she never paid, she worked with Tony Jackson, composer of "Pretty Baby".
77.q: And Hugh Hoskins was Elite Number Two, because I remember the first little diamond ring I got was a little, tiny ring -- the man Tenan (PHONETIC) Jones owned Elite, Numbers One and Two. And he had a little ring, he sold it to me for $40.00, and I never did pay him.
